title: Assembly Language
overview: Assembly language is a low-level language in which each instruction corresponds to one machine-code instruction. Paper 1 gives you the CAIE instruction set and asks you to trace short programs in a trace table, write or complete short programs, identify the addressing mode an instruction uses, and describe how a two-pass assembler turns source code with labels into machine code.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of the relationship between assembly language and machine code.
Describe the different stages of the assembly process for a two-pass assembler.
Trace a given simple assembly language program.

Show understanding that a set of instructions are grouped, including data movement, input and output of data, arithmetic operations, unconditional and conditional instructions, and compare instructions.
Show understanding of and be able to use the immediate, direct, indirect, indexed and relative modes of addressing.

definitions.definition: Instructions in binary that the processor can execute directly.
A low-level language that uses mnemonics and labels, where each instruction translates to one machine-code instruction.
The part of an instruction that specifies the operation to be performed, e.g. LDD or ADD.
The part of an instruction that specifies the data, or the address of the data, to be used.
A translator that converts assembly language into machine code.
A table built by the assembler that records each label and the address it represents.
The way the operand of an instruction is interpreted to find the data to be used.
A table recording the values of the accumulator, registers and memory locations after each instruction is executed.

sections.title: Assembly language and machine code
content: The processor only understands machine code: binary patterns made of an opcode and an operand. Assembly language replaces the binary opcodes with short mnemonics (such as LDD, ADD, JMP) and lets programmers use labels instead of numeric addresses. There is a one-to-one relationship: each assembly instruction becomes exactly one machine-code instruction. Assembly language is specific to one processor's instruction set, so a program written for one processor type will not run on another.
bullets: Assembly language is used where precise control of hardware, speed or small program size matters, e.g. device drivers and embedded systems.
It is harder to write, read and debug than a high-level language.
In the CAIE instruction set, #n is a denary value, Bn is binary and &n is hexadecimal.

sections.title: The two-pass assembler
content: A program can refer to a label before the label is defined, for example jumping forward to a label further down the code (a forward reference). The assembler therefore reads the source code twice. In the first pass it reads each line, removes comments and white space, and adds every label to the symbol table with its address, calculated by counting instructions from the start address. In the second pass it replaces every label with its address from the symbol table, converts each mnemonic into its binary opcode using an opcode table, and generates the machine code (object code). Errors such as undefined labels or unknown mnemonics are reported.
bullets: Pass 1: build the symbol table (labels → addresses).
Pass 2: translate opcodes and replace labels using the symbol table, producing object code.
A single pass would fail on forward references, because the address of a label later in the code is not yet known.

examples.label: Symbol table after pass 1
examples.content:
Program starts at address 100:
100 START: LDD COUNT
101        CMP #0
102        JPE FINISH
103        JMP START
104 FINISH: END
105 COUNT:  5
Symbol table: START → 100, FINISH → 104, COUNT → 105
JPE FINISH is a forward reference: FINISH is only reached later in pass 1.

sections.title: Instruction groups
content: The CAIE instruction set groups instructions by purpose. Data movement instructions copy values between memory, the accumulator and the index register: LDM #n loads a number into the ACC, LDD loads from an address, LDI loads indirectly, LDX loads indexed, LDR #n loads a number into the IX, MOV copies the ACC into another register, and STO stores the ACC to memory. Input and output use IN (read a character and store its ASCII value in the ACC) and OUT (output the character whose ASCII value is in the ACC). Arithmetic instructions are ADD and SUB (with an address or a number), and INC and DEC (add or subtract 1 from the ACC or IX). CMP compares the ACC with an address or a number, and CMI compares indirectly. JMP is an unconditional jump; JPE jumps if the last comparison was equal and JPN jumps if it was not equal. END returns control to the operating system.
bullets: Compare instructions do not change the ACC; they set a flag that the next conditional jump reads.
Conditional jumps are how selection and loops are built in assembly language.
STO copies the ACC into memory; the ACC keeps its value.

sections.title: Addressing modes
content: In immediate addressing the operand is the value itself (LDM #150 puts 150 into the ACC). In direct addressing the operand is the address of the value (LDD 150 loads the contents of address 150). In indirect addressing the operand is an address that holds another address, where the value is found (LDI 150 reads address 150, uses that value as an address, and loads from there). In indexed addressing the operand is added to the contents of the index register to form the address (LDX 150 with IX = 1 loads from address 151). In relative addressing the address is given as an offset from the address of the current instruction, so the code works wherever it is placed in memory.
bullets: Immediate: fastest, but the value is fixed in the program.
Indirect: useful for pointers, where the address of the data changes at run time.
Indexed: ideal for stepping through an array by incrementing IX in a loop.
Relative: makes code relocatable because no absolute addresses are used.

examples.label: One operand, four addressing modes
examples.content:
Memory: address 150 contains 300, address 151 contains 20, address 300 contains 45. IX contains 1.
LDM #150 (immediate) → ACC = 150
LDD 150 (direct) → ACC = 300
LDI 150 (indirect) → address 150 holds 300, so load from 300 → ACC = 45
LDX 150 (indexed) → address 150 + 1 = 151 → ACC = 20

sections.title: Tracing a program
content: To trace a program, draw a table with columns for the instruction address, the ACC, the IX if used, each memory location that changes, and any output. Work through the instructions one at a time, following jumps, and write a new row only when a value changes. Keep track of the result of each CMP so you know whether the next conditional jump is taken.
bullets: Start by writing the initial memory values in the first row.
After a JPE or JPN, write down whether the jump was taken before continuing.
Stop at END; the final row shows the program's result.

examples.label: Tracing a loop that adds a value repeatedly
examples.content:
Initial memory: 200 = 3 (counter), 201 = 0 (total), 202 = 5 (value)
100 LDD 201
101 ADD 202
102 STO 201
103 LDD 200
104 DEC ACC
105 STO 200
106 CMP #0
107 JPN 100
108 END

First pass through the loop (instruction: ACC | 200 | 201):
Start:        – | 3 | 0
100 LDD 201:  0 | 3 | 0
101 ADD 202:  5 | 3 | 0
102 STO 201:  5 | 3 | 5
103 LDD 200:  3 | 3 | 5
104 DEC ACC:  2 | 3 | 5
105 STO 200:  2 | 2 | 5
106 CMP #0: 2 ≠ 0, so 107 JPN jumps to 100

End of each later pass:
Pass 2: ACC 1 | 200 = 1 | 201 = 10 → JPN jumps to 100
Pass 3: ACC 0 | 200 = 0 | 201 = 15 → CMP equal, JPN not taken, END
Result: address 201 holds 15, i.e. 5 × 3.

sections.title: Writing short programs
content: Plan the task in steps first: what must be loaded, what calculation or comparison is needed, where the result is stored, and where the program must jump. Use labels for jump destinations and data locations so the program is easy to follow. Selection is written as a CMP followed by a conditional jump; a loop is a block that ends with a comparison and a jump back to its start.
bullets: An IF is: CMP, conditional jump past the 'then' block, then block, label after it.
A counting loop needs a counter in memory or in the IX, a DEC or INC, a CMP and a conditional jump.
Remember that LDD overwrites the ACC, so store any result you still need first.

examples.label: Output 'Y' if two numbers are equal, otherwise 'N'
examples.content:
LDD NUM1
        CMP NUM2
        JPE YES
        LDM #78      ; ASCII 'N'
        OUT
        JMP DONE
YES:    LDM #89      ; ASCII 'Y'
        OUT
DONE:   END

formulas.label: Relative address
formulas.expression: effective address = address of current instruction + offset

comparisonTable.title: Addressing modes
rows: An address holding the address of the value
A base address added to the IX
An offset from the current instruction's address

diagram.title: Two-pass assembly
nodes: Pass 2: replace labels and translate opcodes

analysisChains.title: Why the assembler needs two passes
steps: A jump instruction may refer to a label further down the program
When the assembler first reaches the jump, the label's address is unknown
Pass 1 records the address of every label in the symbol table
Pass 2 can then replace every label, including forward references, with its address
analysisChains.evaluation: Two passes take slightly longer to assemble but let programmers use labels freely, making code much easier to write and maintain.

analysisChains.title: Using indexed addressing to total an array
steps: The IX is set to 0 and the base address of the array is used as the operand
LDX reads the element at base + IX
INC IX moves to the next element on each pass of the loop
The same few instructions process an array of any length
analysisChains.evaluation: Without indexed addressing, a separate instruction would be needed for each element, making the program longer and unable to handle different array sizes.

analysisChains.title: Writing a routine in assembly rather than a high-level language
steps: Each instruction maps directly to one machine instruction
The programmer controls exactly which registers and memory are used
The code can be very fast and compact, suiting device drivers and embedded systems
But it is slow to write, hard to debug and tied to one processor type
analysisChains.evaluation: Assembly is justified only for small, time-critical or hardware-specific parts of a system; the rest is better written in a high-level language.

examTips: In trace tables, record a new value only when it changes, and show whether each conditional jump is taken.
Read the '#' carefully: LDM #5 loads the number 5, while LDD 5 loads the contents of address 5.
For indirect addressing, look up the memory twice: once to find the address, again to find the value.
When describing the two-pass assembler, name the symbol table and say which pass builds it and which pass uses it.
Use the CAIE instruction set exactly as given in the question paper's table; do not invent mnemonics.
commonMistakes: Treating an immediate operand (#n) as an address.
Forgetting that CMP does not change the ACC.
Stopping an indirect lookup after one step and loading the intermediate address instead of the value.
Missing a jump back to the start of a loop, or taking a JPN when the comparison was equal.
Saying one assembly instruction becomes several machine-code instructions; the relationship is one-to-one.
Forgetting to add the IX when working out an indexed address.

quickRecall.question: What is the relationship between assembly language and machine code?
quickRecall.answer: One-to-one: each assembly instruction translates into exactly one machine-code instruction.

quickRecall.question: What happens in the first pass of a two-pass assembler?
quickRecall.answer: Comments are removed and each label is added to the symbol table with its address.

quickRecall.question: What happens in the second pass?
quickRecall.answer: Labels are replaced by addresses from the symbol table and mnemonics are converted to binary opcodes, producing object code.

quickRecall.question: Address 80 contains 95 and address 95 contains 7. What does LDI 80 load?
quickRecall.answer: 7 (address 80 gives the address 95, whose contents are 7).

quickRecall.question: IX = 3. Which address does LDX 60 read from?
What is the difference between JPE and JMP?
quickRecall.answer: JPE jumps only if the last comparison was equal; JMP always jumps.

quickRecall.question: What does IN do?
quickRecall.answer: Reads a character from the keyboard and stores its ASCII value in the ACC.

quickRecall.question: Why is relative addressing useful?
quickRecall.answer: Addresses are offsets from the current instruction, so the code works wherever it is loaded in memory.
